..
Issued at 158 AM MDT Fri Jul 31 2026

We have finally reached the end of July. And, like many of the past 
months in the past year, it has been a very warm one. Several of our 
climate sites are having their warmest July on record and many 
others are in the top 5. And this looks to continue into the 
weekend. And then, we may finally get some relief from the record 
warmth we have been experiencing. 

It is generally more of the same today. It will be another very warm 
to hot day today, with temperatures a few degrees warmer than 
yesterday. Precipitable water values also drop another 10 to 20 
percent today, finally getting back to near climatological averages. 
However, there is still just enough low and mid level moisture for 
some isolated showers and storms. As for where, the models continue 
to be on the struggle bus when it comes to where they will form. So, 
for now I have just gone with a broad area of slight POPS across 
most of the area, similar to the Storm Prediction Center outlook. 
The chance at most spots is less than 1 out of 5 though and most 
areas will not see one. The main threat from any storm would be 
strong wind gusts given the large dew point depressions. And this 
should be another show where most showers and storms should end
by sunset with all showers done by midnight.

The ridge builds northward over Wyoming over the weekend. This will 
have two impacts. One, with the warming aloft and much drier air, 
the chance of convection will be almost zero. It will also warm 
quite a bit, with 700 millibar temperatures climbing as high as 20 
to 21 degrees celsius. This should push high temperatures in 
locations below 7000 feet into the 90s, with areas below 5000 feet 
likely seeing highs into the triple digits. The peak of the heat 
still looks to be on Sunday. The reason for this will be a 
southwesterly, downsloping breeze that will develop ahead of an cold 
front dropping into Montana. This should add a few degrees to the 
temperatures in the lower elevations, with most locations below 5500 
feet having at least a 3 in 5 chance of high temperatures of 100 or 
higher. The center of the heat looks to be in central Wyoming, 
where the Big Horn Basin from Basin to Thermopolis as well as the 
Wind River Basin below 5000 feet have a 1 in 2 chance of high 
temperatures of 105 or higher. This is the day we could see some all 
time record high temperatures for August. For some locations, this 
could be the third time this calendar year (they also occurred in 
March and July, as well as December of last year). As for 
highlights, we elected to go with heat advisories rather than 
excessive heat warnings. Why? For one, the really hot temperatures 
should only last two days, not four like back in July. In addition, 
the nights are now getting longer so we have a longer period to cool 
off at night. And relative humidity will be very low, as low as 5 
percent. And this lowers the heat index. However, this will lead to 
another possible hazard.

And that hazard is elevated to critical fire weather. Elevated fire 
weather is likely on Saturday with the low humidity. However, wind 
is not expected to be strong and should remain below critical 
levels. It will be a different story on Sunday as the cold front 
approaches and tightens the pressure gradient. It is a bit lighter 
than yesterday, but still has a greater than 1 in 2 chance of gusts 
over 25 mph over portions of the area. We will hold off for now 
since there is still time, but future shifts may have to issue Fire 
Weather Watches starting on Sunday afternoon. 

The aforementioned cold front drops through the area Sunday night 
and Monday, although it will be a slow passage. Temperatures will 
cool East of the Divide on Monday anywhere from 10 to 20 degrees, 
making for a nice, refreshing change from the recent hot weather. 
Southern Wyoming will likely see one more hot day before the front 
sips through Monday night. There is very little moisture with it 
though, so the chance of any showers is basically zero. And with the 
poor humidity recovery and gusty wind around the front, there will 
likely be another day of elevated to critical fire weather, so any 
highlights may end up being multi-day warnings. 

Tuesday may end up being the coolest and most comfortable day, 
possibly a taste of September. Many areas have at least a 1 in 2
chance of high temperatures under 85 degrees, with the warmest 
temperatures in southern Wyoming, where the front will likely 
wash out. The GFS MOS has a high temperature of 65 in Cody on 
Tuesday. This looks way too cool given the early August sun 
angle though. Following this, we should see a gradual warming 
trend, although record warm temperatures look unlikely the rest 
of next week. It also looks rather dry, with any deeper moisture
likely remaining south of Wyoming. So, any chances of 
precipitation look slim for much of next week.
